list.listitem: Per ACC/AHA guidelines, for patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF), anticoagulation is recommended when the CHA2DS2VASc score is 1 or greater in men and 2 or greater in women. Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred due to a lower risk of bleeding.A

Renal function and hepatic function should be evaluated before initiation of therapy with direct thrombin or Factor Xa inhibitors, and should be reevaluated when clinically indicated and at least yearly.B

The 2021 ACCP guidelines recommend a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban) as first line therapy for venous thromboembolism (VTE). Patients with antiphospholipid syndrome should be treated with warfarin. A

If initiating therapy with warfarin for VTE, concomitant initiation of parenteral therapy with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH), fondaparinux, or subcutaneous UFH is recommended for at least 5 days and until the INR is 2.0 or above for at least 24 hours. A

In patients with proximal deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), at least 3 months of anticoagulation is recommended; extended anticoagulation using rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is recommended for those with low/moderate bleeding risk and no provoking factor.A

For selected patients with isolated acute distal DVT, serial imaging is recommended with anticoagulation only if the clot extends proximally. Similarly, for patients with subsegmental PE, no proximal DVT, and who are at low risk for recurrent VTE, clinical observation without anticoagulation is recommended. B

In treatment of VTE in cancer patients, updated ACCP guidelines recommend an oral Factor Xa inhibitor (apixaban, rivaroxaban, or edoxaban) over LMWH. In gastric malignancies, apixaban is less likely than rivaroxaban and edoxaban to increase the risk of GI bleed.B
Warfarin should be used to treat patients with mechanical heart valves to reduce their risk of thromboembolic events. A

Anticoagulation is indicated to prevent thromboembolic disease for those with atrial fibrillation mechanical heart valves and in selected patients with prothrombotic states, such as malignancy. It is also indicated for the treatment of thromboembolic disease. The choice of agents is guided by evidence as well as patient preference, cost, and access to follow-up.
An oral agent that competitively inhibits subunit 1 of vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) complex and decreases vitamin K and synthesis of clotting factors.

Interacts with many medications, including antibiotics; such medications may increase the risk of bleeding or decrease the effectiveness of warfarin (i.e. depending on the medication, may increase or decrease the INR).

If bleeding occurs, vitamin K can be used as a reversal agent. Four factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) can be used to treat major bleeding events when rapid repletion of clotting factors is desirable.
Indirectly bind to antithrombin, thus allowing for inactivation of coagulation factors.
Relatively short-acting and can be given as an infusion that can be started and stopped for procedures.
Given via subcutaneous injection or intravenously.
If bleeding occurs, protamine can be used for neutralization.
Causes antithrombin III inactivation of Factor Xa.
Given as a subcutaneous injection.
If bleeding occurs, protamine can be used for partial neutralization

section.type: Direct Thrombin Inhibitors Dabigatran, Ximelagatran, Hirudin, and Bivalirudin
section.heading: Direct Thrombin Inhibitors Dabigatran, Ximelagatran, Hirudin, and Bivalirudin

list.listitem: Directly inhibit free and fibrin-bound thrombin, thus inhibiting coagulation-mediated effects of thrombin.

If bleeding occurs, idarucizumab can be used for neutralization of dabigatran. While its use has been shown in a case series to reverse anticoagulation promptly, the impact on mortality or bleeding outcomes has not been demonstrated in a trial. Other agents are in development for other direct thrombin inhibitors.
Concomitant use of amiodarone, fluconazole, rifampin, and phenytoin are associated with an increased risk of bleeding complications.

A retrospective cohort study in Medicare beneficiaries found that in patients using oral anticoagulants alone, the risk of hospitalization for upper gastrointestinal tract bleeding is highest with rivaroxaban and lowest with apixaban. Cotherapy with a proton pump inhibitor reduces the risk among patients using any oral anticoagulant. The oral anticoagulants which were compared were rivaroxaban, dabigatran, apixaban, and warfarin.

Using national registries, Canadian researchers concluded that major bleeding complications were more common in patients given clarithromycin compared with azithromycin (0.77% vs. 0.43%, adjusted hazard ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.20-2.45).
The A4C risk score (age, eGFR, hemoglobin, albumin and amiodarone) predicts the risk of major bleeding in older patients taking a DOAC.

section.type: Factor Xa Inhibitors Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban
section.heading: Factor Xa Inhibitors Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban

list.listitem: These drugs selectively and reversibly inhibit Factor Xa, and are given orally. They are highly protein bound and not dialyzable.

Andexanet alfa is a modified recombinant inactive form of human factor Xa that has been approved for reversal of factor Xa inhibitors. While treatment with andexanet alfa reduced anti-factor Xa activity, the reduction in anti-factor Xa activity was not predictive of hemostatic efficacy.
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) may also be used to reverse bleeding due to factor Xa inhibitors.

A retrospective cohort study found that concomitant use of amiodarone with apixaban or rivaroxaban was associated with a greater likelihood of bleeding related complications (57 vs 39 events/1000 person-years).
Benefits:
NVAF increases the risk of stroke fivefold over that of patients in sinus rhythm.

The CHA2DS2-VASc score more clearly defines anticoagulation recommendations and should be used to determine who should receive anticoagulation. For patients with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0 in men or 1 in women and NVAF, it is reasonable to omit antithrombotic therapy. For patients with scores 1 or higher in men and 2 or higher in women, stroke risk is elevated to at least 4% per year, and anticoagulation using a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is recommended by ACCP guidelines.
ACC/AHA guidelines recommend anticoagulation at slightly higher cutoffs for CHA2DS2-VASc of 2 for men and 3 for women.

A systematic review concluded that for patients with AF detected by an implanted device, use of a DOAC lowers the risk of stroke (NNT = 100) but increases the risk of major bleeding (NNTH = 62) and does not affect mortality.

A randomized trial with 1015 patients concluded that anticoagulation with apixaban did not reduce recurrent strokes in patients with recent cryptogenic strokes and evidence of atrial cardiopathy without atrial fibrillation compared with aspirin therapy.
One year after successful ablation, a randomized trial with 840 adults found no advantage of continuing a DOAC.

In patients with AF and concomitant atherosclerosis and previous ischemic neurologic events, a Japanese trial with 316 patients concluded that adding an antiplatelet agent to an anticoagulant led to no benefit and more major bleeding.
Harms:

Anticoagulation increases the risk of bleeding complications. Scoring tools such as HAS-BLED, HEMORR2HAGES, and ATRIA can be used to predict the likelihood of major bleeding. However, all three scores have only a modest performance and poor predictive accuracy.

Bridging anticoagulation during times of surgery or procedures paradoxically may lead to a higher likelihood of cardiovascular and bleeding events with no difference in stroke or thrombotic events. It may still be considered for patients at high risk of thromboembolic events. See Perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy.

A retrospective cohort study found that an INR of greater than 1.5 on admission was independently associated with an increased risk of both in-hospital and 1-year mortality in hospitalized patients treated with DOACs. Compared with patients with an INR of 1.5 or less, those with an elevated INR were more likely to have underlying liver disease (2.6% vs 4.1%).

A study using Medicare data found that among patients taking a DOAC, the upper GI bleeding risk was highest with rivaroxaban (Xarelto) and lowest with apixaban (Eliquis). Cotherapy with a proton pump inhibitor was associated with a significantly reduced risk of UGI bleeding (76 vs. 115 episodes/10,000/year).

Among older adults taking direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), concurrent use of clarithromycin, as compared with azithromycin, is associated with a higher 30-day risk of hospitalization with major bleed. Use of serotonin specific reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) also significantly increased the risk of a major bleeding episode compared with OAC use alone. Risk was highest in the first 30 days of treatment and continued for up to 6 months. Risk was not affected by SSRI type or potency and occurred with both direct oral anticoagulants and vitamin K antagonists.

The concomitant use of amiodarone with a DOAC, compared with either sotalol or flecainide plus a DOAC, by older patients with atrial fibrillation was associated with a higher risk (17 more per 1000 person-years) of bleeding-related hospitalizations.

Valvular AF (AF in the setting of moderate to severe mitral stenosis) or in the presence of a mechanical/artificial heart valve is considered an indication for long term anticoagulation with warfarin, although DOACs are preferred by ACC/AHA guidelines.
If chosen as an anticoagulant for those with atrial fibrillation, warfarin should be initiated with titration in dosing to achieve a goal international normalization ratio (INR) of 2–3.
INR should be monitored at least weekly when initiating anticoagulation and at least monthly when the INR range is stable.

DOACs are recommended over warfarin except in those patients with moderate-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve; also in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome for whom anticoagulant is needed, warfarin is currently preferred.

A study randomized 217 patients to morning vs. evening administration of warfarin. There was no difference in the percent time in the INR range and no different in any clinical endpoints of adverse events.

For patients with atrial fibrillation and rheumatic heart disease, an RCT with 4565 adults found that warfarin was superior for a primary composite outcome of stroke, embolism, MI or vascular death (6.3% vs 8.1%, p = 0.002, NNT = 56).

The most recent AHA/ACC/HRS guidelines for use of antithrombotic agents in atrial fibrillation recommend use of a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) rather than warfarin for most patients with newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation.

Dabigatran at a dose of 150 mg, when compared to warfarin, was associated with slightly lower rates of stroke or systemic embolism (1.1% vs. 1.7%; RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.53-0.82) and similar rates of major hemorrhage (3.1% vs. 3.4%; p = 0.31).

Rivaroxaban was non-inferior to warfarin for the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism in patients with atrial fibrillation, with no difference in the risk of major bleeding and slightly lower rates of intracranial and fatal bleeding.

In patients with atrial fibrillation, apixaban was superior to warfarin in preventing stroke or systemic embolism (1.3% vs. 1.6%; HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66-0.95), caused less major bleeding (2.1% vs. 3.1%; HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.60-0.80), and resulted in a small decrease in all-cause mortality (3.5% vs. 3.9%; HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.35-0.75; NNT 250).

In an observational study of approximately 12,000 patients 65 and older with atrial fibrillation, use of a DOAC was associated with a lower risk of stroke and lower all-cause mortality. The study design is limited in that it cannot adjust for unknown or unmeasured confounders and did not adjust for time in range for the warfarin patients.

DOACs demonstrated superior safety when used in patients with cancer and AF. Warfarin had higher mortality and risk of hemorrhagic stroke, while the risk of ischemic stroke was similar between warfarin and DOACs.
A trial using Medicare registry data found the highest risk of UGI bleeding with rivaroxaban and the lowest with apixaban. Co-treatment with a PPI is associated with a lower risk of UGI bleeding.

For patients with stable coronary artery disease and atrial fibrillation, an RCT with 2215 adults concluded that monotherapy with rivaroxaban is preferable to rivaroxaban plus a platelet inhibitor one year after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or bypass surgery. Not only were there fewer deaths (NNT = 66/year), there were fewer hemorrhagic strokes (NNT = 312) and fewer major bleeding events (NNT = 88).

An RCT studied a high-risk group of patients with atrial fibrillation and acute coronary syndrome or the need for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). In these patients, apixaban plus clopidogrel without aspirin provided the best balance of benefits and harms. Triple therapy that adds aspirin cannot be recommended on the basis of these results.

A recent meta-analysis comparing standard dose DOACs to warfarin across various ages and sex found DOACs to have statistically significantly lower risk of stroke and systemic embolism, death, and intracranial bleeding than warfarin. Difference in major bleeding was not statistically significant. Lower dose DOACs had no statistically significant decrease in risk of stroke and systemic embolism, but lower risk of death, intracranial bleeding, and major bleeding than warfarin.

A study randomized 1006 patients with ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation to early resumption of a DOAC within 48 hours for minor or moderate strokes and 6-7 days for major stroke, or to to initiation 3 days after minor stroke, 6 days after moderate, and 12 days after severe stroke. Mean age was 77 years, and 37% had minor stroke, 40% moderate, and 23% severe. Primary composite of stroke, embolization, bleed, or death occurred less often in the early initiation group (2.9% vs 4.1%). There was no increase in the risk of symptomatic intracranial bleeds (0.2% in each group).

A study randomized 888 patients with acute ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation who were not taking a DOAC at the time of the stroke to early initiation of a DOAC (0-4 days) or late initiation (5-10 days). The primary composite of new ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, or death occurred less often in the early start group (6.9% vs 8.7%) and, although noninferior, this difference was not significantly lower (superior). Further study is needed in the subset of 121 patients who were undergoing thrombectomy, as those in the early initiation group had a nonsignificantly higher rate of the composite outcome (12.3% vs 3.6%).

An individual patient meta-analysis found a mixed bag of potential benefits and harms from anticoagulation in patients with atrial fibrillation and a previous history of ICH. There were fewer ischemic cardiovascular events (4% vs 19%; NNT = 7) with the use of a DOAC, but a concerning increase in all-cause mortality in the single largest trial (NNTH = 9). Once again, this is an opportunity for shared decision-making. The authors note that 5 additional studies are underway with results expected in approximately 5 years.

The most recent ACCP guidelines on anticoagulation for NVAF recommend a direct oral anticoagulant over warfarin for most patients due to a slightly lower risk of bleeding, and recommend anticoagulation for men with a CHA2DS2VASc score of 1 or more and for women with a score of 2 or more. The ACC/AHA guidelines recommend anticoagulation for men with CHA2DS2VASc score of 2 and for women with a score of 3; they further state that anticoagulation may be considered in scores of 1 and 2 respectively.

Renal function and hepatic function should be evaluated before initiation of therapy with direct thrombin or Factor Xa inhibitors and should be reevaluated when clinically indicated and at least yearly.

For patients with end-stage renal disease, a CHADS2-VASc score of 2 or greater, and with creatinine clearance <15 mL/min or who are on hemodialysis, warfarin titrated to an INR of 2–3 is a reasonable choice.

For patients with valvular atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban is noninferior to warfarin for the prespecified composite outcome. Although designed as a noninferiority trial, there were significantly fewer strokes in the rivaroxaban group (number needed to treat [NNT] = 56 over 1 year).

Among patients presenting with pulmonary embolism (PE), the rate of fatal PE during anticoagulant therapy was 1.5% (95% CI 0.9%-2.2%) all deaths occurred during the first two weeks of anticoagulant treatment. Following anticoagulant therapy, it was 0 per 265 patient-years (95% CI 0-3.6), an NNT of 67 to prevent one death per 265 patient-years. The case-fatality rate of recurrent DVT or PE among patients presenting with PE was 26.4% (95% CI 16.7%-38.1%).
In patients with PE, approximately 3% who are treated go on to develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; treatment with anticoagulation is recommended when compared to stopping therapy.

For selected patients with isolated acute distal DVT, serial imaging is recommended with anticoagulation only if the clot extends proximally or there are severe symptoms. Similarly, for patients with subsegmental PE, no proximal DVT, and who are at low risk for recurrent VTE, clinical observation without anticoagulation is recommended.
Among patients anticoagulated for VTE, the risk of major bleeding is 7.2 events per 100 person-years and the risk of fatal bleeding is 1.3 per 100 person-years.
Among those who receive anticoagulation therapy for more than 3 months, the case-fatality rate for an episode of major bleeding is approximately 9%.
In patients being treated with anticoagulation for acute VTE, the concomitant use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or aspirin is associated with an increased risk of bleeding.

A meta-analysis of four trials looked at the subset of patients also taking aspirin, and concluded that if a patient must take aspirin, patients randomized to a DOAC instead of warfarin had fewer strokes or VTEs (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.69-91), fewer vascular deaths (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76-0.93), and a trend toward fewer major hemorrhages (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69-1.01).
Warfarin has been the mainstay of treatment since the 1960s.

The only RCT comparing treatment of DVT or PE with warfarin to no treatment included only 35 patients. The trial was halted after there were five deaths among 19 in the untreated group, compared with none in the 16 who were anticoagulated.

If initiating therapy with warfarin for VTE, concomitant initiation of parenteral therapy with an LMWH, IV unfractionated heparin (UFH), fondaparinux, or subcutaneous UFH is recommended for at least 5 days and until the INR is 2.0 or above for at least 24 hours.
summarizes the benefits and harms of direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) compared with warfarin.
Apixaban has a slightly lower risk of major bleeds and no difference in efficacy when compared with enoxaparin and warfarin treatment.
Rivaroxaban had a lower risk of recurrence of VTE and no difference in all-cause mortality or in major bleeding as compared with enoxaparin or warfarin treatment for DVT.
An RCT in children with VTE compared dabigatran with standard therapy. Dabigatran was non-inferior to standard therapy.
For patients with VTE, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or edoxaban are preferred over a VKA such as warfarin. LMWH may be used in individuals with inability to take oral medications.

Renal and hepatic function should be evaluated before initiation of therapy with direct thrombin or Factor Xa inhibitors, and should be reevaluated when clinically indicated and at least yearly. Edoxaban should not be prescribed for patients with normal renal function (creatinine clearance >95 mL/min), as they clear the drug too quickly. In a large trial, the risk of stroke was significantly increased in these patients.
For patients with end-stage renal disease or with creatinine clearance <15 mL/min, or who are on hemodialysis, warfarin to an INR of 2–3 is a reasonable choice.

Choosing an anticoagulant is based on multiple factors: warfarin is cheaper but requires monitoring and has a small increase in bleeding risk as compared with apixaban. DOACs require no special monitoring; however, they are more expensive than warfarin and sometimes require twice-a-day dosing (as with dabigatran and apixaban or the first 21 days of rivaroxaban). Patient preference and financial considerations must be taken into account.
In patients with acute proximal DVT, isolated distal DVT of the leg, or PE, that is provoked by surgery or nonsurgical transient risk factor, 3 months of therapy with anticoagulation is recommended.

In patients with first unprovoked DVT or PE and a low to moderate risk of bleeding, extended anticoagulaton therapy using apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily is recommended by the 2021 ACCP guidelines. This has only been studied in clinical trials for 2 to 4 years. If a decision is made to discontinue extended anticoagulation, these patients should be placed on low dose aspirin.
In patients with first unprovoked DVT or PE and high risk of bleeding, at least three months of anticoagulation therapy is recomended.
A meta-analysis of 16 studies generally supports a prolonged period of anticoagulation of 6 months to 2 years for patients with unprovoked VTE, in particular unprovoked PE.
In patients with unprovoked acute proximal DVT or PE, who are stopping anticoagulation therapy, use of aspirin is suggested to prevent recurrent VTE, if there are no contraindications to aspirin use.
In patients with recurrent VTE, anticoagulation therapy for an indefinite period reduced the rate of recurrence as compared with 6 months of therapy.

In certain populations (women with unprovoked DVT or PE without a high risk of bleeding), D-dimer values can be helpful in determining the risk of recurrence. The risk of recurrence in women with a negative post-treatment D-dimer appears to be similar to the risk for patients with a proximal DVT or PE that was provoked by a minor transient risk factor (approximately 15% recurrence at 5 years). Consequently, the argument for extended anticoagulation in these women is not strong. The same is not necessarily true for men, and no absolute recommendation can be made as a whole yet on using D-dimer measurements.

section.type: Anticoagulation for VTE Prophylaxis in Hospitalized Patients
section.heading: Anticoagulation for VTE Prophylaxis in Hospitalized Patients

list.listitem: The benefits of preventing a VTE have to be weighed against the harms of causing a bleed in hospitalized patients. ACP guidelines recommend selective use of VTE prophylaxis based on an assessment of risk.
PE accounts for 5%–10% of deaths in hospitalized patients, making VTE the most common preventable cause of in-hospital death.

Groups at high risk of VTE include post-operative patients and those with medical conditions that predispose them to VTE, such as malignancy, previous VTE, reduced mobility, and heart failure. This risk can be reduced with VTE prophylaxis.
Several thrombosis risk assessment scoring systems have been developed, including Geneva, Padua, Kucher, IMPROVE, and Intermountain, but further validation is needed.

Patients with COVID-19 are at a high risk for thrombotic events including stroke, VTE and MI and are routinely treated with anticoagulants at either prophylactic or therapeutic doses, although randomized trials are lacking.
Enoxaparin at a dose of 40 mg daily is a viable option for VTE prophylaxis in patients with normal kidney function.
Subcutaneous heparin dosing for VTE prophylaxis is appropriate in preventing mortality in immobilized medical patients who are not at risk of bleeding.

A systematic review concluded that aspirin is no different than other anticoagulants for the prevention of VTE following total hip replacement (THR) or total knee replacement (TKR) and does not increase the number of adverse events. The majority of the studies included in this meta-analysis were at high risk of bias and there was heterogeneity between studies, suggesting that further research is needed to confirm these findings.

section.type: Recurrent DVT in Patients Who are Anticoagulated
section.heading: Recurrent DVT in Patients Who are Anticoagulated

list.listitem: In patients who experience a recurrent VTE while being treated with either a DOAC or VKA therapy (and have been compliant), changing anticoagulation therapy to LMWH is recommended. Dose increase is recommended for patients who experience a recurrent VTE while being treated with a LMWH.
ACOG guidelines recommend LMWH as the preferred anticoagulant during pregnancy. Though UFH is a reasonable choice, LMWH is preffered because of greater reliability and ease of use.
Warfarin is a known teratogen and should not be used in pregnancy, though in patients with mechanical valves, may be considered in concert with multidisciplinary team after the first trimester.
DOACs should not be used during pregnancy; there is a lack of data documenting safety.

Per recent CHEST guidelines, individuals with superficial venous thrombosis should be given 2.5 mg fondaparinux daily for 45 days if at increased risk for DVT or PE progression. Conditions which confer increased risk include extensive SVT (particularly over 5 cm), involvement above the knee, severe symptoms, involvement of the greater saphenous vein, previous history of VTE or SVT, active cancer, or recent surgery. Rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 45 days is an acceptable alternative for those who refuse or can't take fondaparinux.
Ultrasound should be performed on SVT above the knee to rule out DVT.

A Cochrane Review concluded that prophylactic dose fondaparinux (2.5 mg daily) given for 45 days appears to be a valid therapeutic option for ST of the legs for most people. This was based on findings of reduction in symptomatic VTE, superficial thrombosis (ST) extension, and ST recurrence.
For cancer patients with an episode of VTE, apixaban, edoxaban, and rivaroxaban are recommended over low-molecular-weight heparin by 2021 ACCP guidelines.

Consider a longer period of anticoagulation. A trial randomized patients with cancer and VTE to 18 vs 6 months and found fewer (mostly asymptomatic) episodes of VTE but numerically more bleeds with longer duration of anticoagulation. Another study found that low-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) had a similar benefit with less bleeding when given for 18 months to patients with cancer and VTE.

A clinical trial randomized 1046 patients with cancer and an episode of VTE to edoxaban or dalteparin (after a 5 day initial treatment with a LMWH). The likelihood of subsequent VTE was similar (12.8% vs. 13.5%, p = ns), although there were more major hemorrhages in the edoxaban group (6.9% vs 4.0%, p = 0.04, NNTH = 34). Most of the hemorrhages were GI bleeds in patients with gastrointestinal cancer.

In an RCT of 1155 patients with active cancer, apixaban was as safe as, and noninferior to, dalteparin for the treatment of venous thromboembolism. The easier administration and trend toward fewer recurrences are likely to make it the preferred agent.

An RCT with 563 patients found that apixaban used as primary thromboprophylaxis is effective in preventing VTE in patients with active cancer—who are at higher risk for VTE—and are starting chemotherapy. You would need to treat 17 such patients with apixaban to prevent one VTE over 6 months. A higher incidence of major bleeding was seen with apixaban, mostly in patients with gastrointestinal and gynecologic cancers (number needed to treat to harm = 59).

Another trial that compared rivaroxaban with placebo in the same patient population did not show a decrease in VTEs during the pre-specified 180-day follow up; however, the high medication discontinuation rate in this study likely affected the outcomes. During the 4.3 month intervention period, however, there was a significant reduction in the primary endpoint (composite of lower extremity DVT, upper extremity DVT, pulmonary embolism, and death).

A trial randomized 671 cancer patients with symptomatic or asymptomatic VTE randomized them to a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) or LMWH. DOAC numerically better and non-inferior to LMWH (6.1% vs 8.8% VTE). At 6 months adherence was also better in the DOAC group (71% vs 59%).

A randomized trial of 178 patients with active cancer and a low risk PE to 6 versus 18 months of DOAC. The 18 month group had fewer episodes of PE or DVT (5.6% vs 19.1%, NNT = 7) but most were incidentally discovered. There were only 4 symptomatic VTE in the 6 month group and 0 in the 18 month group after 18 months of follow-up.
A Cochrane systematic review of 20 studies with 9771 cancer patients concluded that LMWH and UFH were similarly effective for perioperative thromboprophylaxis.

A Cochrane review of anticoagulation for persons with cancer and a central venous catheter concluded that LMWH reduces the risk of VTE but not mortality. The potential benefits must be balanced with the increased risk of bleeding.

A Cochrane systematic review of patients with cancer but no indication for anticoagulation found no reduction in mortality with anticoagulation, but there was an increase in the risk of major bleeding.
Danaparoid (in a therapeutic dose) and argatroban infusion are acceptable alternative anticoagulants for the treatment of patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (HITT).
Fondaparinux and the DOACs are reasonable alternatives in otherwise stable patients (i.e. not at risk of loss of life or limb)

section.type: Anticoagulants for Patients with Mechanical Valve
section.heading: Anticoagulants for Patients with Mechanical Valve

list.listitem:
ACC/AHA guidelines (2020) continue to recommend that warfarin or another vitamin K antagonist should be used to treat patients with mechanical valves in order to reduce their risk of thromboembolic events.
The target INR for mechanical aortic valve is 2.5, but if a patient has risk factors including atrial fibrillation, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction, or hypercoagulable state, target should be 3.0 The target INR for mechanical mitral valve is 3.0, as MV has higher likelihood of thromboembolism than aortic valves
Dabigatran is not recommended for mechanical valve anticoagulation due to an excess risk of strokes and bleeding compared with warfarin. Additional trials are ongoing.

ACC/AHA guidelines (2020) recommend the following for patients who have had a bioprosthetic valve replacement:
Bioprosthetic transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI): aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily Bioprosthetic surgical aortic or mitral valve replacement (SAVR): aspirin 7 to 100 mg daily. For those at low risk of bleeding consider a vitamin K antagonist with a target INR of 2.5 for the first 3 to 6 months post-operatively. For patients with bioprosthetic TAVI, low dose rivaroxaban 10 mg plus aspirin 75 to 100 mg is contraindicated in the absence of other indications for these medications. Following a thromboembolic event in a patient with a bioprosthetic aortic or mitral valve replacement, VKA anticoagulation is recommended.

A randomized trial of 865 patients undergoing TAVI who were on long-term anticoagulation. Compared with interruption of therapy, continuation of anticoagulation for patients undergoing TAVI using long-term anticoagulant therapy may lead to more bleeding and vascular complications without the benefit of reducing thromboembolic events. Based on this study, holding anticoagulation prior to the procedure is recommended.

For patients with a bioprosthetic mitral valve and atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban was noninferior to warfarin for the prespecified composite outcome in an RCT with 1005 patients. Although designed as a noninferiority trial, there were significantly fewer strokes in the rivaroxaban group (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.88, NNT = 56 over 1 year).

The ongoing PROACT-Xa clinical trial will compare the safety and effectiveness of apixaban vs. warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves, but currently factor Xa inhibitors are not recommended in patients with mechanical heart valves

A meta-analysis compared vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin with DOACs for patients who have undergone transcatheter aortic valve implantation. They identified 8 studies with 25, 769 patients and found no difference for all cause mortality, stroke, or major bleeding. The likelihood of any bleeding was lower in the DOAC group (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.76-0.91).

For patients with subsegmental PE (no involvement of more proximal pulmonary arteries) and no proximal DVT in the legs, who have a low risk for recurrent VTE, it is appropriate to suggest clinical surveillance over anticoagulation. For patients with a high risk for recurrent VTE, it is appropriate to suggest anticoagulation over clinical surveillance. High risk patients include those who are hospitalized or have reduced mobility for another reason, have active cancer (particularly if metastatic or being treated with chemotherapy), or have no reversible risk factor for VTE such as recent surgery or immobilization. Furthermore, a low cardiopulmonary reserve or marked symptoms that cannot be attributed to another condition favors anticoagulant therapy, whereas a high risk of bleeding favors no anticoagulant therapy.

As stated above, the choice of anticoagulant from the evidence-based options is based largely on patient preference. Edoxaban should not be prescribed for patients with a creatinine clearance of >95 mL/min as they clear the drug too quickly for it to be effective.

Initiating anticoagulation treatment as an outpatient is recommended in patients with DVT and low risk PE, who are expected to be compliant with treatment, feel well enough to be treated at home, have no contraindications (recent bleeding, severe renal/liver disease or severe thrombocytopenia) and have the ability to be promptly hospitalized if necessary.
When initiating therapy with warfarin for stroke prevention in patients with NVAF, bridging with UFH or LMWH is not necessary.

If initiating therapy with warfarin for VTE, concomitant initiation of parenteral therapy with LMWH, intravenous UFH, fondaparinux, or subcutaneous UFH is recommended for at least 5 days and until the INR is 2.0 or above for at least 24 hours.
Warfarin dosing should be monitored with INR checks to a target goal based on indication, which is 2–3 for atrial fibrillation and VTE and is usually 2.5–3.5 for mechanical valves.

In patients with atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin, interruption of warfarin and no initiation of bridging therapy as compared to bridging therapy in patients undergoing an elective operation or other elective invasive procedure showed a decrease in bleeding (RR 0.41; 95% CI 0.20-0.78) and no difference in arterial thromboembolism. This may not apply to patients at very high risk of thromboembolism or high procedural bleeding risk.

Genotype-guided warfarin dosing in patients following knee or hip arthroplasty was compared with standard algorithm for dosing. There were fewer patients whose INR was > 4, but no significant differences in rates of death, bleeding, or VTE.
Oral vitamin K lowers INR more rapidly than subcutaneous Vitamin K in asymptomatic patients who have supratherapeutic INRs while on warfarin therapy.
Heparin reversal can be achieved with the use of protamine, while LMWH can be partly neutralized by protamine.
Dabigatran neutralization can be achieved with idarucizumab. While its use has been shown in a case series to reverse anticoagulation promptly, the impact on mortality has not been demonstrated.
Andexanet alfa is used to reverse Factor Xa inhibitors activity if bleeding occurs. 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) can also be used to reverse anticoagulation due to DOACs.

A meta-analysis concluded that use of aspirin, clopidogrel, and dual antiplatelet therapy at the time of non-cardiac surgery only increase the risk of bleeding complications slightly (RR for transfusion 1.14 for aspirin, 1.33 for DAPT).
